book: 104 - Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!

chapters.file: ch03 - Per Aspera ad Astra—Through the Thorns to the Stars.md

chapters.relation: The editors' introduction argues that Red Rising grips because it mirrors our own world of class struggle, where a Gold-like elite lives in luxury on the backs of oppressed laborers kept distracted by games and propaganda. It traces Darrow's arc from resigning himself to death after Eo's execution, through his carving and campaign of destruction, to the discovery that friendship with Sevro, Mustang, Victra, and Ragnar—not revenge—is what actually pulls him out of life's mines. It closes by previewing the volume's questions: whether enhancement could doom humanity, whether Darrow is the same person after the carving, love versus vengeance, how society should be structured, and the meaning of life.

chapters.file: ch08 - I. Conundrums for the Quality Control Board.md

chapters.relation: Tim Jones argues the Golds misread Darwin: they take themselves to be the perfected endpoint of natural selection and use the Passage and Institute to 'help Nature along' by culling weaker Golds, justifying the subjugation of lower Colors—the same social-Darwinist logic Hitler and Stalin used to dress up atrocity. Using Darwin's own contrast between natural selection and man-made selective breeding, he shows the Institute is an artificial arena and the Golds' shaping of Reds and Pinks is self-serving husbandry, not nature's work. The twist is that the very traits the Golds bred into lowReds—Helldiver knuckles, miner's endurance, drill-floor courage—are what win Darrow the Institute, the Iron Rain, and the fight against the Jackal, so their manipulated evolution becomes the tool of their own extinction, just as Quicksilver's case against the static Color hierarchy implies.

chapters.file: ch10 - 2. Not So Human After All.md
chapters.relation: Brendan Shea takes the Jackal's claim that Golds and Reds are separate species (Homo flameus versus Homo sapiens) seriously and tests it first against Aristotle's essentialism—species fixed by necessary properties, complete with the doctrine of natural slaves—and then against three modern species concepts (Mayr's interbreeding criterion, the phylogenetic common-ancestry view, and the ecological-niche view), showing each gives the Jackal ambiguous or inconvenient verdicts, from sterile Pinks to horizontal gene transfer. He concludes with Peter Singer that moral equality never depended on equal intelligence or strength: Reds have interests just as Golds do, so enslaving them would be wrong even if Adrius were right about the biology. The deeper lesson is that the Jackal reasoned backwards from his commitment to Gold rule, finding whatever differences his prejudice needed—a warning against 'discovering' biological support for pre-existing biases.

Kevin McCain asks whether Darrow the hero and Nero au Augustus the villain can really be told apart, noting both hold noble goals (Eo's dream versus preserving humanity) and share brutal means. Consequentialism fails to separate them: Darrow's sacrifice of dockworkers and Sons of Ares to Romulus mirrors Nero's 'I do what I need to do to protect the greater good,' and Harmony's sacrificing Evey shows the same ends-justify-means reasoning. Kantian ethics condemns both, since each lies to people and sacrifices them without consent, treating them as mere means to an end. Virtue ethics finally offers grounds: Aristotle's requirement of proper motivation, developed through Michael Slote, distinguishes Darrow, who acts from love for Eo, his friends, and the Colors and is wracked by guilt, from Nero, who is fueled by inhuman pride and feels nothing at Eo's hanging—so motivation may be what makes one forgivable and the other a villain, though the chapter ends wondering if good intentions pave the road to Hell.

Trip McCrossin reads Darrow's storyline as an engagement with the problem of evil in both its theological form (Harmony dubbing him Lazarus, the parables of John and Luke) and its secular form, which Susan Neiman traces to the Rousseau-Voltaire dispute: must evil be made intelligible or not? Darrow begins Voltairean—incredulous before the rigged Laurel and Eo's hanging ('She left me')—but his resurrection and political awakening on the surface remake him Rousseauian: evil is the misalignment of individual and general wills, and humans are corrupted by society, not born bad. The chapter reads Darrow's 'Man was born free' broadcast in Morning Star, his new social contract with Victra, and the education of Pax (with Lysander left to Cassius to 'raise him right') as Rousseau's Social Contract and Emile program—break the chains, then educate each generation so its contracts align ever closer with the general will.

chapters.file: ch13 - 5. The One, the Only, Darrow.md
chapters.relation: Kevin McCain uses Darrow's transformations—Helldiver of Lykos, carved Gold lancer, Reaper of Mars—to ask what makes him numerically the same person, warming up with Plutarch's Ship of Theseus replayed on the Pax and the Quinn trading parts. Same-matter and animalist views (Eric Olson) struggle with Mickey's near-total carving and Darrow's restarted heart, and Locke's prince-and-cobbler example, run as a carver swapping Darrow's and the Jackal's psychologies, sinks all physical-continuity views. The simple memory theory breaks transitivity across Darrow's childhood, and Sydney Shoemaker's psychological-continuity fix then fails when a carver splits Darrow's brain into two surviving bodies—a fission case where both new Darrows continue him—while the soul view cannot be verified; the chapter ends with Trenton Merricks's suggestion that there may be no criteria of identity over time at all.

chapters.file: ch14 - II. Searching for Eo’s Dream.md
ch15 - 6. Driven by Love to Go to War.md
chapters.relation: John Karavitis deploys Alain Badiou's account of love as a contingent encounter founding the 'Two scene'—seeing the world from the perspective of difference—to argue that Darrow and Eo were never truly in love: their glade conversation, his 'nobility of obedience' against her 'live for more,' was two monologues, and you cannot love a memory. He then diagnoses Darrow as a narcissist in Rousseau's sense of amour-propre—self-love turned vanity that lies to itself—whose quest serves to manage his shame at failing to protect Eo, citing Erich Fromm on narcissism's path to fascism and Aristotle on habituation into Gold ways. Only the Jackal's stone-table imprisonment shatters the narcissism ('Man is no island'), letting Darrow embrace agape, with Ovid's Echo and Narcissus and the haemanthus framing the trilogy as a warning against self-love.

Courtland Lewis asks who Darrow is—Red, Gold, hybrid, savior—and surveys theories of the self: Plato's immortal soul ruling the body, Descartes's cogito as thinking thing, and Hume's denial that introspection ever reveals more than a stream of perceptions (we never experience a soul, only thinking). Freud's id-ego-superego offers a secular soul, but Sartre carries the chapter: Darrow is being-for-itself, perpetually projecting what he is not, tortured by the Look of others—Eo seeing a savior, Mustang holding him at gunpoint, Roque's betrayed friendship—and prone to bad faith through 'guardrails' like the Vale, excuses about Eo and Uncle Narol, and pining for Mustang instead of owning his choice. Since existence precedes essence, Darrow is nothing but the sum of his free choices, and to live otherwise is to choose slavery.

Kevin McCain separates meaning of life—why humans exist at all, with no creator-God found in Gold nihilism ('the Golds have no God'), the Obsidians' manufactured Norse religion, or the Reds' Vale and Old Man—from meaning in life, following Susan Wolf's distinction. After rejecting supernaturalism and pessimistic naturalism (Nero's universe that 'does not notice us,' met by Karnus's Camus-like defiant pride and Thomas Nagel's ironic stance), he rejects Richard Taylor's subjectivism via the Sisyphus story: Karnus and the Boneriders enjoy their cruelty, but enjoying it does not make their lives meaningful. Wolf's objectivism wins—a meaningful life is actively and lovingly engaged in projects of worth—which is exactly Darrow's living for more, contrasted with the Jackal's loveless, self-loathing pursuit of mattering.

chapters.file: ch18 - III. To Live or Not to Live in the Society.md

chapters.relation: Randall Jensen maps the Society onto Plato's Republic (Brown has said he drew on it): the Color hierarchy parallels the Myth of the Metals' gold, silver, and bronze souls, the Golds' scorn for Demokracy echoes Book VIII's account of degeneration into tyranny, and Leto's 'We are Plato's philosopher kings' claims a mantle Plato himself doubted anyone could ever fill. Darrow's story is the Allegory of the Cave run from below—a Helldiver literally raised in a mine, blinded by surface light, whose return to a shrunken, grayer garden mirrors the philosopher's homecoming—except Plato never imagined the prisoner carved into a Gold. The Noble Lie survives as the terraforming myth fed to lowReds while the surface has been habitable for centuries, and the chapter weighs Darrow's gospel ('we choose who we are') against Plato's caveats: you can choose who to be only within limits, if you are lucky and greatly helped.

Darci Doll argues the Rising exposes the Society's intellectual oppression—each Color denied education and fed 'noble lies' about its role—and that lifting it sparks an 'Intellectual Reformation' proving Color does not dictate potential: Darrow out-performing Golds, Orion the un-carved Blue, Ragnar and Sefi exceeding their station. She uses Plato's Republic (producers, auxiliaries, guardians, the lower orders kept obedient by Noble Lies like the Reds' terraforming myth) as the Society's blueprint, then turns to Aristotle: potential is realized only through the right environment, instruction, and habituated character, and Darrow's practical wisdom—testing himself, reassessing after Titus and Cassius, doing what makes him his best self—lets him flourish and lead. Aristotle's critique of utility-only relations explains why the Society's alliances expire (Antonia executed once useless) while Darrow and Mustang's virtue friendships and just rule endure, opening a society where everyone, including women and lowColors denied opportunity rather than ability, can maximize potential.

chapters.file: ch21 - 11. Beautiful Colors and Unjust Societies.md
chapters.relation: Devon Brickhouse-Bryson asks whether the Society, plainly dystopian with respect to justice, might nonetheless be utopian with respect to beauty. Treating a society as an abstract object—a system of persons ordered into a community, not reducible to its members or its gravBoots and razors—and beauty as harmoniousness, the ordering of parts into a unified whole in the tradition of Aristotle, Aquinas, and Hutcheson, he shows the Color system straightforwardly instantiates that definition, each caste an organ of one well-functioning clock. But the harmony holds only if the castes are genuinely teleologically distinct; if that is mere Gold propaganda, the Society is not beautiful but a cacophony. Either way the chapter's real lesson stands against Plato: identifying justice with each part fulfilling its role conflates beauty with justice, and the Society shows how radically the two can come apart—possibly beautiful and radically unjust at once.

chapters.file: ch22 - 12. The Law of Red Rising.md
chapters.relation: Christopher Ketcham frames the Society through jurisprudence's debate between natural and positive law, opening with Gramsci's hegemony: Reds have internalized the Golds' message that their slave toil is heroic terraforming service, becoming 'enabled martyrs' who hate rival clans rather than their rulers. He deploys Hobbes's state of nature versus state of laws (Reds live in a state of war against Mars while Golds legislate in a state of law), Locke's suggestion that a sovereign can leave some people in the state of nature, Aquinas-style higher law, and H.L.A. Hart's positivism with Bentham and Austin—a law need not be moral to be law—to argue the Golds' caste statutes are valid yet ungrounded. His coda casts Darrow as Homer Plessy: Goldness, like whiteness in Plessy v. Ferguson, is inheritable property Reds cannot claim, and because Reds who speak are hanged, the law excludes the very voices Hart himself said keep laws from becoming terrible.

chapters.file: ch23 - IV. The Rising and Beyond.md

chapters.relation: Courtland Lewis asks what Mustang owes future generations when rebuilding the Society, first showing that standard moral theories stall: nonexistent people lack rationality, cannot contract, cannot be treated virtuously, and utilitarian forecasting fails since we cannot know whether the Jackal's nuking of Luna might have led, in the deep future, to prosperity. Derek Parfit's Reasons and Persons then strikes: any policy choice creates a different future generation, total utility drives the Repugnant Conclusion (a maximally populous world of barely-worth-living lives, uncomfortably like the Society's Reds), and average utility yields the mere addition paradox (Mustang's Society is both no worse off and worse off when Andromeda's low-pleasure civilization is added). The chapter's solution is Rawls: the original position behind the veil of ignorance—where the Sovereign would not know she is a Gold—yields justice as fairness and maximin reasoning for the just savings problem, choosing to save more than is consumed; against Tim Mulgan's objection that this loops back to the Repugnant Conclusion, Lewis answers that real carrying capacities make the repugnant world impossible.

chapters.file: ch25 - 14. Guns Don’t Kill Colors—Colors Kill Colors.md
chapters.relation: Robert Arp argues from Hobbes's right of nature—self-preservation as the first law found out by reason—that individuals, and by extension oppressed peoples, have a right to the means of lethal defense, so arming the lowColors of the Society is justified. He weighs pacifist counterpoints (Augustine on self-defense as inordinate self-love, the Buddhist first precept, Camus's refusal to kill) and answers with Aquinas's principle of double effect: Darrow destroying the flagship to save Luna, intending the good while foreseeing the deaths, is justified, as is killing in defense of innocent children the Institute rapes and eats. The Society then illustrates why disarmament enables tyranny—Hideyoshi's Sword Hunt, Stalin's weapons bans, the Golds' razor monopoly—so that when lowColors finally receive weapons in Morning Star they become the means by which the police state falls: guns equalize the weak against aggressors and the people against the state.

The Bocks trace Darrow's education out of vengeance: in Plato's tripartite soul the spirited part (anger) must obey reason, and Aristotle's virtue of mildness—anger at the right things, toward the right people, for the right length of time—is the golden mean between slavish and irascible that Darrow has not yet reached. Darrow learns the difference when he hands Titus over to Cassius's vendetta and admits 'That wasn't justice': retribution in Kant's lex talionis tradition must be dispassionate and proportional, while vengeance is past-oriented and insatiable, and Darrow's own bombing of the Ganymede docks shows how troubling even his 'justice' remains. Against Darrow's violent justice-in-love the chapter sets Martin Luther King Jr.'s agape and loving-forgiveness—Sevro hanging and then forgiving Cassius, Darrow forgiving Tactus, Mustang pulling her brother's legs for a merciful death—closing with King's warning that constructive ends can never justify destructive means, and Darrow's own admission that 'the war is not over.'

chapters.file: ch27 - 16. Can We All Get Along.md
chapters.relation: Courtland Lewis tackles transitional justice after atrocity: with the Rising won, what is to be done with millions of Golds complicit in slavery, rape, and torture? He tests Peter French's virtuous vengeance—punishment that fits the wrong, grounded in Locke's natural rights—and finds Darrow's destruction of Gold society fails it (disproportionate, unsober, punishing young Julian for his ancestors' crimes), then turns to Jessica Wolfendale's argument that declaring anyone unforgivable adopts the wrongdoer's own devaluing outlook, exactly as Darrow becomes what he despises. The working model is South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission—confession, conditional amnesty, truth-telling, reparations, Tutu, Mandela, Beth Savage hoping to meet her bomber—applied to Mars through Mustang-style dignified engagement on Adam Michnik's model and Slavenka Drakulic's lesson that every Color inherits responsibility for rejecting the Society's past.

chapters.file: ch28 - Guide to the World of Red Rising.md
ch30 - Howlers, Helldivers, and Peerless Scarred.md

holes.name: Charles Darwin
holes.what: Naturalist whose On the Origin of Species (1859) explains evolution through natural selection and contrasts it with man-made selective breeding.
holes.why: Chapter 9's entire argument—that the Golds misapply natural selection, run the Institute as artificial selection, and are undone by the traits they bred into Reds—is built directly on Darwin's own distinctions and text.

holes.name: Species Concepts (biological, phylogenetic, ecological)
holes.what: The philosophy-of-biology debate over what fixes a species—interbreeding (Mayr's Biological Species Concept), common descent, or adaptation to an ecological niche—replacing Aristotelian essentialism.
holes.why: Chapter 10 tests the Jackal's claim that Golds and Reds are separate species against each of these three species concepts, none of which the taxonomy covers.

holes.name: Voltaire (François-Marie Arouet)
holes.what: French Enlightenment satirist whose Candide, through Dr. Pangloss's best-of-all-possible-worlds optimism, argues morality demands we not pretend evil is intelligible.
holes.why: Chapter 12 stages Darrow's development as a move from the spirit of Voltaire (evil stays unintelligible) to the spirit of Rousseau, with Candide receiving extended treatment.

holes.name: Alain Badiou
holes.what: Continental philosopher for whom love is one of four truth procedures: a contingent encounter that founds the 'Two scene' of seeing the world from the perspective of difference (In Praise of Love).
holes.why: Chapter 15's central claims—that Darrow and Eo were never truly in love and that Darrow and Mustang only become a couple at the trilogy's end—are argued entirely through Badiou's account of love.

holes.name: Beauty as Harmoniousness (unity in variety)
holes.what: The classical tradition (Aristotle, Aquinas, Hutcheson) defining beauty as the appropriate, coherent ordering of an object's parts into a unified whole.
holes.why: Chapter 21 asks whether the Color society is beautiful precisely by applying this harmony definition of beauty, and the taxonomy has no concept for beauty or aesthetics generally.

holes.name: Legal Positivism (law and morality separate)
holes.what: The view associated with Bentham, Austin, and H.L.A. Hart that a law's validity is one thing and its moral merit another: law is what is posited, with hard cases forming a penumbra.
holes.why: Chapter 22 weighs the Golds' legal order as valid positive law against natural law, and the taxonomy has no slug for legal positivism or the Hart-side of the debate.

holes.name: The Repugnant Conclusion (population ethics)
holes.what: Parfit's result that total utilitarianism favors a vast population of lives barely worth living over a smaller, happier one, with the mere addition paradox haunting average-utilitarian views.
holes.why: Chapter 24's argument about Mustang's obligations to future generations runs entirely through the Repugnant Conclusion and the mere addition paradox, which the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
holes.what: Civil-rights leader whose philosophy of agape, loving-forgiveness, and nonviolent resistance is set out in Stride Toward Freedom, Strength to Love, and The Trumpet of Conscience.
holes.why: Chapter 26 measures Darrow's violent Rising against King's nonviolent alternative, quoting King's accounts of agape, forgiveness, and the ends-preexistent-in-the-means throughout its second half.

holes.name: Transitional Justice
holes.what: The truth commissions, conditional amnesties, reparations, and dignified engagement by which societies move from large-scale atrocity to mutual cooperation instead of mass punishment.
holes.why: Chapter 27 argues the post-Rising Society needs exactly a Truth and Reconciliation-style process for the Golds, and the taxonomy has no transitional-justice concept.
